questions.prompt: Match each boundary form to its defining property.

pairs.right: Reciprocal interfaces + DTOs + two managed components (max independence and cost)
All interfaces and DTOs, but kept in one component
A single (Strategy-style) interface instead of reciprocal ports
A clean entry point that delegates to concretes — no dependency inversion

questions.explanation: Boundary strength and cost decrease from a full boundary, through skip-the-last-step and a one-dimensional interface, to a facade (which provides no inversion). Full boundaries cost the most, so you don't build them everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which partial boundary provides NO dependency inversion?
questions.explanation: A facade depends on the concrete services and clients depend on the facade, so no dependency is inverted; it tidies structure but doesn't buy independence.

questions.prompt: The partial boundary that creates all the interfaces and DTOs but keeps everything in a single component is called 'skip the last ______'.
questions.explanation: 'Skip the last step' saves the cost of managing two components while leaving the code ready to split later.

questions.prompt: Which of these are partial-boundary techniques (cheaper than a full boundary)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skip the last step (interfaces/DTOs in one component)
A full reciprocal boundary with two managed components

questions.explanation: Skip-the-last-step, one-dimensional boundaries, and facades are partial boundaries — cheap seams you can strengthen later. A full reciprocal boundary with two components is the full (most expensive) form, not a partial one.

questions.prompt: Order these partial-boundary options from strongest/costliest to weakest/cheapest.

items.text: Skip the last step (interfaces/DTOs, one component)

questions.explanation: Cost and strength decrease from a full boundary, to skip-the-last-step, to a one-dimensional interface, to a facade.

questions.prompt: Is deciding which boundaries to build a one-time, up-front task?

options.text: No — it's ongoing; watch for friction and strengthen boundaries when the cost becomes justified
Yes — the framework decides for you
No — you should never revisit a boundary

questions.explanation: Martin stresses this is ongoing judgment: watch for real friction (a second implementation, scaling, team splits) and strengthen boundaries then — avoiding both over- and under-engineering.
